page_title: Inside Atlassian: how site reliability engineers do incident management

summary.name: Atlassian SRE incident management process
summary.one_liner: A blog post by Atlassian's head of site reliability engineering describing how the SRE team handled a 2016 Confluence Cloud incident that broke page editing, and the incident management process they follow.
use_cases: Designing an incident response process for an engineering team
Learning how to run an incident manager on-call rotation
Setting up log-based anomaly detection with an ELK stack
Routing alerts to on-call engineers via PagerDuty
summary.what_it_does: The post is a first-person account of how Atlassian's SRE group responded when a 2016 Confluence Cloud release stopped users from editing pages. It describes the team's monitoring, including alerts sent to HipChat and on-call phones via PagerDuty, and an ELK-based log analytics system called Logging As A Service for spotting unusual errors. It explains the incident manager on-call role, which coordinates responders rather than fixing the problem, and the four steps used: keep people informed, restore service quickly, capture everything, and learn and improve through a blameless post-incident review. The worked example traces how the team found that disabling Atlassian Connect for affected users restored the editor while a proper fix was developed.
notable: Incident manager on-call role focused on coordination rather than technical fixes
Real example: disabling Atlassian Connect for affected users restored Confluence editing
Logging As A Service built on Elasticsearch, Logstash and Kibana to surface unknown problems
Four-step incident process ending in a blameless post-incident review
caveats: Describes Atlassian's internal tooling and practices circa 2016 (HipChat, Jira Service Desk); tools may have changed since
Not a product; it is an article describing internal processes
